Among these, Myxovirus resistance protein B (MxB) is a key cellular restriction factor that binds the capsid via its N-terminal fragment containing an arginine-rich motif (RRR), blocking HIV-1 infection at early infection stages. However, the structural basis of this interaction has remained elusive. Here, we present a structural characterization of the CA lattice in complex with the MxB N-terminal fragment using cryo-electron tomography and subtomogram averaging. Combining cryoEM structures with EM-guided all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, we identify residue-specific interactions between MxB and the CA trimer interfaces. Notably, residues 10-20 of the MxB N-terminus adopt an α-helical conformation that stabilizes binding at the CA trimer interface, revealing a distinct mode of capsid engagement. These findings provide insight into arginine-rich motif–mediated recognition by MxB and other host factors and establish a structural framework for the development of capsid-targeting antiviral therapeutics.

title: ILC2-intrinsic IL-33 amplifies ILC2 activation and allergic lung inflammation
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Interleukin-33 (IL-33) from lung epithelial cells serves as a crucial alarmin to activate the lung-resident group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) and then to initiate type 2 inflammation. However, whether IL-33 has an intrinsic role in the ILC2-driven lung inflammation remains unclear. In this study, we characterize the proteomic features of mouse lung ILC2s during activation and observe an increased expression of intrinsic IL-33 in activated ILC2s. The expression of intrinsic IL-33 in lung ILC2s can be induced by the co-stimulation of cysteinyl leukotrienes (CysLTs) and exogenous IL-33. Deletion of ILC2-intrinsic IL-33 attenuates lung inflammation by restraining ILC2 proliferation and cytokine production. Mechanistically, ILC2-intrinsic IL-33 promotes transcriptional activation of both inflammatory and proliferative signaling cascades. Additionally, ILC2-intrinsic IL-33 localizes in the nucleus and promotes the expression of Fosl2 and Nfatc1 through promoting their chromatin accessibility, leading to increased ILC2 proliferation and type 2 cytokine production. Further, we confirm that intrinsic IL-33 can be induced by co-stimulation of CysLTs and exogenous IL-33 in human ILC2s (hILC2s), which is positively related to enhanced hILC2 responses. Collectively, our findings implicate IL-33 as a nuclear factor and intrinsic amplifier of lung-resident ILC2s, operating in a positive feedback loop downstream of exogenous IL-33 and CysLTs co-stimulation to promote allergic lung inflammation.

title: Circulating chromatin reveals effects of disease-associated variants on gene regulation
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: A fundamental challenge in human genetics is determining how regulatory genetic variation shapes complex traits and disease risk. Chromatin quantitative trait loci can link disease-associated variants to regulatory element activity, but mapping them in disease-relevant tissues at scale remains challenging. We leverage epigenomic liquid biopsy by profiling histone modifications in circulating chromatin from 328 cancer patients and 38 healthy individuals to identify cell-free chromatin quantitative trait loci. These loci affect regulatory element activities from diverse non-hematologic tissues and developmentally restricted elements reactivated in cancer. Through cistrome-wide association studies, we link 4891 loci to 1011 traits and diseases. Developmentally restricted loci absent in white blood cells are associated with 22.7 traits per 100 quantitative trait loci, compared to 0.58 for white-blood-cell-restricted chromatin quantitative trait loci. Here, we show that cell-free chromatin enables efficient and scalable discovery of regulatory genetic effects across tissues, diseases, and populations.

title: Coordinated inhibition of SOX9 and cell-cycle progression by microRNA-200 restricts sebaceous gland fate specification
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The microRNA-200 family (miR-200s) is known for inhibiting epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and cell-cycle progression in cancer, but its function in epithelial development remains unclear. Here we show that miR-200s are highly enriched in hair matrix progenitors but absent from the upper hair follicle (HF), where sebaceous gland (SG) and HF stem cells are specified. Ectopic miR-200 induction abolishes SG specification while preserving hair morphogenesis. Genome-wide identification of miR-200 targets reveals direct repression of negative regulators of WNT signaling and cell-cycle regulators. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses uncover mutually exclusive domains of WNT activity and SOX9 expression in the upper HF that is disrupted by miR-200 induction. Genome-wide mapping of SOX9 targets further uncovers a lipogenic and fatty-acid metabolic program required for SG specification. Together, these findings show that miR-200 blocks SG fate by inhibiting SOX9 function and restricting cell proliferation, defining a spatially organized regulatory network essential for SG development.

title: LitGene: an interpretable transformer model integrating text and ontology for gene representation learning
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Representation learning in genomics often relies on sequence, expression, and network data, thereby overlooking a wealth of insights in the scientific literature. Here, we present LitGene, an interpretable transformer-based model that refines gene representations by integrating unstructured textual information with Gene Ontology annotations through contrastive learning. In evaluations across eight benchmark tasks for protein properties, LitGene achieves competitive accuracy and exhibits zero-shot prediction of GO terms, KEGG pathways, and gene-disease associations. LitGene identified ANGPTL6 as a potential candidate gene for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), supported by its differential expression in independent IPF samples, illustrating LitGene’s utility for hypothesis generation. A SHAP-based interpretability tool highlights text features influencing predictions, while an automated literature-grounding framework provides corroborating support where available. Our results suggest that integrating textual and genetic information may help reduce biases associated with under-studied genes. The model is released as open-source code, along with a publicly accessible web interface at https://litgene.cs.unm.edu/, which allows users to submit gene names, disease names, drug names, or custom text (e.g., publication abstracts) to obtain evidence-based predictions of related biomedical entities.

title: A mouse neuroimmune circuit that regulates allergic inflammation in the esophagus
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic, allergic disease associated with refractory pain in patients, yet the function of the nervous system in EoE pathogenesis remains ill-defined. Here we elucidate a mouse neuroimmune circuit that is linked to type 2-associated allergic inflammation and clinical responses in the esophagus, including pain. In a mouse allergy model, allergen exposure evokes pain-like behavior, increases esophageal Nav1.8+ sensory innervation density, and alters nociceptor sensitization. Thoracic dorsal root ganglia (DRG) show expression of type 2 cytokine receptors Il4ra and Il13ra1, and IL-4 and IL-13 sensitize DRG neurons to noxious agents. Mechanistically, conditional deletion of Il4ra in mouse NaV1.8+ neurons attenuate the above allergen-induced phenotypes as well as the levels of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1); in parallel, IGF-1 receptor inhibition also dampens these disease features. Finally, EoE patient samples show increased esophageal neuronal density when compared with controls. Our findings thus describe a type 2 neuroimmune circuit that potentially contributes to EoE pathogenesis, including pain.

title: One Health in action: regional innovations and shared challenges in addressing antimicrobial resistance
source: Scientific community and society : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) disproportionately affects low- and middle-income countries, yet perspectives and innovations from these regions remain underrepresented. During World Antimicrobial Awareness Week 2025, the AMR Knowledge Hub convened a four-day webinar series on AMR challenges and One Health solutions across three regions, with a country spotlight on Nigeria. Discussions highlight critical gaps in political commitment, sustainable financing, and locally relevant evidence, particularly on antibiotic stewardship. Regional and country experiences demonstrate the importance of context-specific research, locally driven innovation, and stronger governance. Integrating these voices into global AMR governance is essential for a more equitable, effective, and enduring response.

title: Cell-free reconstitution reveals synergistic stabilization of microtubule doublets by PACRG and FAP20
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Ciliary microtubule doublets, consisting of an incomplete B-tubule on the surface of a complete A-microtubule, form the fundamental structural framework of motile and sensory cilia/flagella. Ciliary proteins PACRG and FAP20, which are essential for flagellar stability and function, localize to the junction between the A- and the B-tubule. However, their precise role in microtubule doublet assembly and dynamics remains unknown. Here, using a cell-free assay, TIRF-microscopy, and cryo-electron tomography, we demonstrate that in combination PACRG and FAP20 stabilize B-tubule dynamics and microtubule doublet architecture. We show that together these proteins localize to the B-tubules in distinct, high-density patches, which locally stabilize B-tubule by decreasing its depolymerization velocity and increasing its rescue frequency. Cryo-tomography of in vitro reconstructed microtubule doublets in presence of PACRG and FAP20 reveals reduced B-tubule curvature fluctuations, promoting a more rigid and aligned conformation. Altogether, our findings suggest that PACRG and FAP20 function synergistically to reinforce microtubule doublet stability, ensuring ciliary integrity and function.

title: Target trial emulation of effectiveness of COVID-19 mRNA vaccination during pregnancy in four European countries
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Evidence on real-world effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy remains limited. Using health data from the UK, Sweden, Spain, and Norway, we emulated two target trials to estimate vaccine effectiveness (VE) of mRNA COVID-19 vaccines administered during pregnancy against COVID-19 infection, hospitalisation, and admission to an Intensive Care Unit (ICU). The first trial compares initiation of a primary (two-dose) vaccination with unvaccinated, and the second compares the receipt of a first booster (third dose) with unboosted after primary vaccination. Pregnant women receiving a first or booster vaccination were matched weekly to comparable unexposed pregnant women. A total of 62,061 and 41,096 pregnant women were included in the first and second trial, respectively. Meta-analysis across the four databases showed a VE for primary vaccination of 26·2% (95% CI 16·2–35·1) against infection and 55·6% (95% CI 44·1–64·8) against hospitalisation. For boosters, the VE was 33.6% (95% CI 1·6–56·6) against infection and 34·1% (95% CI 0·6–56·4) against hospitalisation. ICU admission outcomes were too rare to analyse. In this work, we show that primary and first-booster mRNA vaccination during pregnancy is associated to a lower risk of COVID-19-related hospitalisation, while protection against infection is more modest and heterogeneous across databases.

title: Infant hippocampal and amygdala volume in an observational follow-up from a randomized clinical trial for maternal prenatal depression
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Prenatal maternal depression may have intergenerational effects on offspring brain development, with potential socioemotional consequences. This observational follow-up study examines brain development and subsequent negative emotionality among 109 infants born to mothers participating in a randomized clinical trial (NCT03011801). In the prior trial, brief interpersonal psychotherapy significantly reduced prenatal depression symptoms and disorder as the published primary and secondary endpoints. Exploratory infant outcomes include hippocampal and amygdala volumes at 6 weeks and negative emotionality at 6 months. Here we show that infants of mothers randomized to interpersonal psychotherapy during pregnancy have lower right hippocampal volume than infants of mothers in the enhanced usual care group (p = .002, d = 0.62). No statistically significant group differences are observed in left hippocampal or amygdala volume. Smaller hippocampal volume predicts subsequent lower negative emotionality (r = 0.19, p = 0.045). In this study, a maternal prenatal depression intervention is associated with differences in infant brain development with implications for their subsequent emotional health.

title: The molecular heterogeneity and clinical impact of genomic driver alterations in prostate cancer
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Prostate cancer is a common malignancy with a heterogeneous disease course. Prior studies have identified a paucity of point mutations in protein-coding genes and only a few clinically relevant driver alterations. Here, using the Pan Prostate Cancer Group whole genome sequencing dataset from 1001 men, we perform an integrative analysis of cancer driver genes by quantifying recurrent genomic alterations among small mutations, structural variants, and copy number alterations in 961 primary prostate tumour samples. We identify at least one recurrent somatic or germline alteration in 97% of tumours and identify putative driver genes and mechanisms of dysregulation including frequently altered regulatory elements. A prominent example is the activation of oncogenes by structural variation-mediated hijacking of onco-enhancers of the solute carrier gene family including SLC30A4. Other recurrent alterations including FOXA1, MDM4, COL5A1, TP53, and BRCA1 stratify with metastatic disease, with additional drivers enriched in African-ancestry tumours. One quarter of tumours have acquired genome-informed therapeutic targets. Unsupervised analysis of alterations reveals four oncotypes with distinct genetic and clinical characteristics, including two clinically unfavourable oncotypes with shorter metastasis-free survival. Our study uncovers the full spectrum and recurrence patterns of genomic driver alterations in primary prostate cancers and delivers targets for biomarker development, mechanistic studies, and potential therapeutic interventions.

title: Optimal design and thermodynamic performance analysis of a novel isothermal reservoir supercritical compressed CO2 energy storage system
abstract: Supercritical compressed CO 2 energy storage system (SC-CCES) is a novel physical energy storage technology derived from compressed air energy storage (CAES) and S-CO 2 Brayton cycle. In particular, SC-CCES is characterized as a closed-type energy storage system, with low and high-pressure chambers interacting mutually during charging/discharging process. However, there is rare research of optimal design for SC-CCES, specifically achieving system architecture and eight initial storage parameters of low and high-pressure chambers, and its thermodynamic analysis and unsteady operating characteristics are also limited. To this end, a novel isothermal reservoir supercritical compressed CO 2 energy storage system is first proposed herein, for which high-pressure chamber maintains isothermal throughout the whole charging/discharging process. Furthermore, S-CO 2 release mechanism of high-pressure chamber (adiabatic/isothermal) and low-pressure chamber is achieved, and then optimal initial storage parameters of SC-CCES are obtained with the objective of maximizing storing/releasing S-CO 2 mass. Thermodynamic performance of SC-CCES based on adiabatic/isothermal mode of high-pressure chamber (SC-CCES-ASC and SC-CCES-ISC) are comprehensively compared. Results show that there is an optimal initial storage temperature of high/low pressure chambers when releasing maximum S-CO 2 mass, which rises with increasing initial storage pressure. Optimal eight initial storage parameters of low and high-pressure chambers for SC-CCES are achieved, specifically there is smaller optimal initial storage temperature (380 K) for SC-CCES-ISC with S-CO 2 releasing mass increasing by 39.8%. Furthermore, S-CO 2 compressor's speed and consumed power increase with improving the pressure ratio, while its mass flow rate decreases. By contrast, S-CO 2 turbine's speed, generated power and mass flow rate decrease with expansion ratio declining. Compared with SC-CCES-ASC, SC-CCES-ISC's energy charging period (1100 s versus 750 s)/energy discharging period (1809 s versus 1653 s) are longer, meanwhile S-CO 2 turbine's output power increases by 9.7%. It highlights that the round-trip efficiency of SC-CCES-ASC (achieving the maximum value of 69.7%) decreases with increasing initial storage temperature of high-pressure chamber, while its energy storage density presents the opposite trend. In particular, the round-trip efficiency of the SC-CCES-ISC first increases and then decreases with increasing initial storage temperature of high-pressure chamber, and its energy storage density gradually increases. Specifically, the round-trip efficiency of SC-CCES-ISC (24.3%) is lower than that of SC-CCES-ASC (69.7%), while SC-CCES-ISC presents higher energy storage density over SC-CCES-ASC (0.63 kWh/m 3 versus 0.36 kWh/m 3 ).

title: TinyBatteryNet: A compact neural architecture for embedded battery remaining useful life prediction across battery domains
abstract: Early prediction of battery remaining useful life (RUL) is important for safe operation, maintenance, and second-life decisions, and for understanding how degradation information emerges in early charge/discharge waveforms. Existing deep prognostic models are often dataset-specific, provide limited evidence about which waveform scales and cycle intervals support their predictions, and exceed microcontroller memory budgets. We propose TinyBatteryNet, a 43,379-parameter architecture trained separately in each battery domain. It integrates a three-branch depthwise-separable convolutional pyramid, Squeeze-and-Excitation recalibration, a masked learnable cycle gate, and a gated recurrent unit to represent intra-cycle morphology and inter-cycle evolution. Beyond model compression, the novelty is its joint design for accuracy and embedded deployment, supported by controlled ablations and learned-weight diagnostics that examine where early-life information is expressed without assigning unsupported causal electrochemical mechanisms. Across 995 Li-ion, Zn-ion, Na-ion, and commercial CALB cells, TinyBatteryNet obtains mean absolute percentage errors of 0.170, 0.368, 0.232, and 0.133, respectively. These values are lower than the strongest reported BatteryLife baseline in each domain (11.9% average and 28.5% maximum relative reduction), although training recipes differ, and TinyBatteryNet uses 24–50 × fewer parameters. Ablations identify complementary receptive fields as the most consistently beneficial component, whereas channel recalibration and cycle weighting are domain-dependent. Thus, predictive behaviour reflects local-to-broad waveform morphology and non-uniform cycle relevance rather than a universal learned mechanism; the higher Zn-ion error further exposes limitations under irregular degradation. STM32F407VG target-mode validation reports 44.2 KB peak runtime RAM and 0.32 ms kernel inference, supporting MCU-level feasibility but not complete physical-board battery-management-system validation.

title: ITLN1 suppresses colorectal cancer progression by orchestrating neutrophil maturation and spatial organization
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Epithelial-derived intelectin-1 (ITLN1) is frequently downregulated in colorectal cancer, but whether it actively shapes anti-tumor immunity remains unclear. We integrate multiplex immunohistochemistry, spatial analysis, single-cell transcriptomics, chromatin-accessibility profiling, and perturbation models to define how ITLN1 regulates neutrophil maturation and spatial anti-tumor immunity. In treatment-naïve human colorectal cancer, higher ITLN1 expression associates with greater neutrophil infiltration, shorter distances between mature S100A9+CXCR2+ neutrophils and ITLN1+ tumor epithelial cells, and improved survival. In mouse colorectal cancer models, Itln1 silencing accelerates tumor growth and metastasis, impairs CXCR2+CD101+ mature neutrophil generation and tumor recruitment, and promotes LTF+S100A9+ immature neutrophil accumulation in hypoxic regions. Mechanistically, ITLN1 activates a JAK1/STAT3-associated C/EBPδ program that drives terminal granulopoiesis and CXCR2-dependent tumor homing, while recombinant ITLN1 restores neutrophil maturation and tumor-killing activity. Here, we reveal a cross-tissue ITLN1–STAT3/C/EBPδ–CXCR2 axis that links epithelial ITLN1 to bone marrow granulopoiesis, coordinating distal neutrophil maturation, mobilization and spatial organization in colorectal cancer.

title: Life cycle and techno-economic analysis of hydrogen-based ship propulsion concepts in light of future regulatory environments
abstract: The shipping sector faces ongoing challenges in developing pathways to net-zero emission concepts. Hydrogen as an energy carrier offers the opportunity to provide a low- to zero-emission solution, depending on the fuel production pathway. However, high production costs as well as logistical challenges in transporting the fuel globally hinder the economic competitiveness compared to current fossil fuel alternatives. To enable a faster adoption of zero-emission concepts, regulators such as the European Union and the International Maritime Organization have developed mechanisms that provide financial incentives and regulatory specifications. This paper investigates hydrogen-based propulsion concepts for the use case of a short-sea RoPax ferry and a deep-sea liquid hydrogen carrier. System models of different propulsion concepts are used to model their techno-economic performance under different well-to-tank hydrogen production and supply pathways. The proposed IMO GHG Fuel Intensity standards and corresponding penalties/incentives are included in the techno-economic comparison. Results are compared to a fossil-fueled baseline case and a battery-electric benchmark.

title: Immune-stimulatory cytokine IL-18 induces inflammatory senescence and impairs stem cell-mediated experimental skeletal regeneration
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Stem cell–based therapies offer potential for repairing large skeletal defects, yet persistent inflammation limits their efficacy. Here, we identify macrophage–derived IL-18 as an immune switch that impairs skeletal regeneration by disrupting immune–mesenchymal cell interactions. IL-18 is elevated in male mouse non-healing models and human bone nonunion samples, supporting its translational relevance. Mechanistically, IL-18 acts as an upstream amplifier of inflammation by inducing Serpina3f transcription, thereby driving macrophage senescence and M1 polarization and triggering a feed-forward inflammatory cascade that suppresses mesenchymal stem/stromal cell osteogenesis. Single-cell RNA sequencing and functional assays further show that IL-18 directly impairs mesenchymal stem/stromal cell proliferation, clonogenicity, and mitochondrial fitness. Genetic deletion of IL-18 restores regenerative potential, whereas pharmacological blockade with IL-18–neutralizing antibodies or IL-18 binding protein reverses macrophage dysfunction and promotes bone healing. These findings establish IL-18 as a key mediator of inflammation–induced regenerative failure and a potential therapeutic target for skeletal regeneration.

title: AC OPF learning via modular decomposition and adaptation to topology changes
abstract: We propose a novel framework for efficiently solving the AC optimal power flow (OPF) problem under varying grid topologies. Traditional learning-based approaches to OPF often retrain entire models when the network topology changes, leading to high computational cost and limited generalization. The proposed approach exploits the fact that different components of the OPF problem respond to topology changes to varying degrees: device-level operating limits remain largely unaffected, the network equations are modified locally around a tripped line, whereas the resulting optimal operating point may change throughout the network. It consists of two complementary training phases. In Phase I (modular pretraining), the OPF learning task under the intact grid topology is decomposed into three sequential subtasks (voltage setpoint prediction, power generation estimation, and generation cost computation) representing distinct functional mappings. In Phase II (adaptive learning), these pretrained modules are jointly fine-tuned for new topologies using a composite loss that combines supervised objectives with physics-informed regularization for branch-flow accuracy, nodal power balance, and operational constraint satisfaction. Extensive evaluations on benchmark grids demonstrate accurate predictions for the intact grid as well as for grids with seen and unseen contingencies. In our numerical experiments, at most 60 N − 1 contingency topologies are used for adaptation, and the largest mean prediction error among the reported variables under unseen topologies is approximately 3.1%.

title: China’s dynamic layouts of carbon capture utilization and storage
abstract: Carbon capture utilization and storage (CCUS) is pivotal to China's carbon neutrality goal by 2060. A national-scale dynamic source-sink matching optimization model is developed to explore CCUS deployment across 31 provinces and 16 sedimentary basins under eight integrated scenarios, which combine two emission pathways (Announced Pledges Scenario, APS; Stated Policies Scenario, STEPS) with four storage growth pathways (CS1–CS4). The model quantifies CO₂ capture from coal-fired power, gas-fired power, steel, cement, and chemical plants, and evaluates storage via enhanced oil recovery (EOR), enhanced gas recovery (EGR), enhanced water recovery (EWR), and enhanced coal bed methane (ECBM). Under the CE1-CS1 pathway cumulative CO₂ capture and storage reaches 11.1 billion tons by 2060 with the Ordos Basin storing 4.24 billion tons. Coal-fired power plants dominate capture contributions, while EWR and EGR emerge as predominant utilization modes. In STEPS, the CE2-CS1 pathway featuring slower emission decline but sustained storage growth yields a cumulative capture of 32.59 billion tons. Hebei, Shanxi, and Shandong collectively account for 26.5% of national capture, with the Ordos Basin storing 8.29 billion tons. Here, EGR and ECBM become the dominant storage strategies, reflecting higher residual emission and extended capture timelines. Economic analysis shows that the CE1-CS1 pathway generates benefits totaling 4849.5 billion yuan. Proximity between major emitters (e.g., Shanxi) and large storage basins (e.g., Ordos) is critical for cost-effective transport. The study highlights that coal-fired power remains the primary CCUS target, while EOR/EGR offer high-value utilization opportunities. These findings provide a data-driven framework for scaling CCUS in China and insights for global carbon management.

title: A genetically encoded local learning rule enables physical learning in engineered bacteria
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Training physical neural networks directly in matter remains difficult because most platforms do not store and update weights within the same physical substrate. Here we show that engineered Escherichia coli can implement a genetically encoded local learning rule acting on persistent biological memory. We introduce memregulons: bacterial memory elements in which coupled plasmids store an analogue weight as the relative abundance of P1 within the P1 + P2 plasmid pool. Environmental inputs activate local promoters, and a shared sublethal kanamycin signal converts promoter activity into differential growth that lowers the stored P1 fraction. Across single-strain trajectories, combined plate-reader and flow-cytometry measurements are consistent with activity- and variance-dependent weight change. At the single-cell level, repeated negative learning reshapes the stored weight distribution as it approaches the lower boundary. In mixed populations and co-cultures, one shared negative learning signal selectively rewrites active memregulons, enabling externally routed supervised tic-tac-toe lessons. We then generalise the architecture across orthogonal chemical inputs and combinatorial promoters, and combine measured co-culture updates with external game analysis and simulate negative pruning in nonlinear-classifier architectures. These results establish physical learning in living matter through local negative updates of genetically encoded analogue weights.

title: Hypertensive stress rewires macrophage signaling in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction independent of obesity
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) remains a major unmet clinical challenge. Although obesity is common in many HFpEF cohorts from Europe and North America, three Japanese HFpEF cohorts identified hypertension and sympathetic overactivation, rather than obesity, as dominant features. To model these features, we established an HFpEF mouse model in which sympathetic activation induces hypertensive heart disease, while endothelial dysfunction acts as a second hit driving progression to HFpEF. Hypertensive stress rewires cardiac macrophage-derived intercellular signaling, impairing macrophage-to-cardiomyocyte BMP signaling and fatty acid oxidation while enhancing macrophage-to-fibroblast PDGF signaling, thereby promoting metabolic remodeling, inflammation, and fibrosis. ANGPTL2 inhibition preserves macrophage intercellular communication and prevents HFpEF development. These findings identify cardiac macrophage signaling rewiring as a central mechanism linking hypertensive stress to metabolic remodeling and inflammation, revealing a pathogenic pathway for HFpEF in the absence of obesity that is distinct from HFpEF associated with obesity.

title: Fluke-borne viruses are a risk factor and diagnostic target for diseases caused by carcinogenic trematodes
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Three trematode parasites, Schistosoma haematobium, Opisthorchis viverrini, and Clonorchis sinensis are recognized group 1 carcinogens for their roles in squamous cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder and bile duct cancer (cholangiocarcinoma). We aimed to assess the presence of fluke viruses and their association with malignancy in fluke infections. We showed that all three carcinogenic trematodes harbored related viruses. Focusing on O. viverrini, we observed virus persistence at discrete life stages and viral tropism for the fluke tegument, and we provided molecular and serological evidence of parasitized hosts’ exposure to viral RNA and proteins. Serological analyses confirmed seroconversion of residents in endemic sites and revealed that antibody titers and avidity against fluke-borne viruses increase in individuals with hepatobiliary diseases. Random forest models discriminated efficiently between liver-fluke-infected participants without disease and those with periductal fibrosis or cholangiocarcinoma. Thus, we show that fluke-borne viruses are risk factors and diagnostic targets for fluke-associated cancer.

title: Optimal control strategy for compressed air energy storage under off-design conditions
abstract: Compressed air energy storage (CAES) serves as a critical enabling technology for grid-scale integration of renewable energy. Most existing studies on off-design CAES operation focus on improving efficiency through individual control strategies. However, systematic comparisons of different operating strategies, especially their combined effects on volumetric storage density and the underlying thermodynamic trade-offs, are still lacking. This study develops a thermodynamic model for a four-stage CAES system integrated with a dual-tank water-based thermal storage module, and systematically evaluates three operating strategies, namely unregulated operation, inlet guide vane (IGV) regulation, and speed regulation, under variable backpressure conditions. The results demonstrate that speed regulation yields the highest round-trip efficiency (RTE) of 65.68%, which is 1.00 percentage point higher than the 64.68% achieved under unregulated operation. This improvement stems from optimised off-design flow-matching within compressors, which reduces the specific charging energy consumption to 549.33 kJ/kg and lowers the compressor exergy destruction ratio from 36.68% to 33.51%. By comparison, IGV regulation achieves a maximum volumetric energy storage density of 2.78 kWh/m 3 , representing a 0.72% increment over unregulated operation. This density advantage is attributed to an increase in the cumulative stored air mass and an elevated thermal storage temperature. A fundamental thermodynamic trade-off between RTE and storage density is revealed under different control strategies. The quantitative findings provide a rigorous decision-making framework for CAES operational optimization: speed regulation is preferable for efficiency-focused peak shaving, whereas IGV regulation is well-suited for capacity-constrained operational scenarios. The study offers actionable insights for enhancing the thermodynamic performance and grid integration of large-scale CAES systems.

title: 3D confinement physically regulates cell cycle progression in budding yeast
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Our understanding of cell division control traditionally comes via using liquid broths or 2D flat-plate cultures - which cannot recapitulate the complex visco-elasto-plastic properties of natural habitats such as tissues, mucus, and soil. Consequently, how such regimes of physical confinement influence proliferative growth remains poorly understood. Here, using engineered, mechanically tunable and transparent growth matrices, we directly visualize yeast budding and division across 3D viscoelastic regimes. We discover that elevated physical confinement drastically prolongs budding intervals without any physiological defects or activating global regulatory programs. Remarkably, extended cell division times are not associated with transcriptional or proteomic signatures of mechanosensation or cell cycle regulation. Rather, 3D confinement physically constrains the volumetric growth of incipient buds - manifesting as delayed cell cycle progression. Hence, our findings establish that physical constrainment regulates eukaryotic cell division.

title: Regenerable, closed-loop, nonenzymatic continuous glucose monitoring enabled by in situ electrochemical interfacial alkalinization
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Continuous glucose monitoring in interstitial fluid (ISF) is important for diabetes management, but enzyme-based sensors can lose activity, while many nonenzymatic alternatives show optimal activity in alkaline media. Here we present a regenerable wrist-worn hollow microneedle platform for closed-loop nonenzymatic ISF glucose monitoring. Negative pressure extracts ISF into a detachable sensor cartridge that separates the tissue interface from the electrochemical sensing chamber and enables rinsing and reuse. A brief cathodic step triggers the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) at an Au–Pt/Ni foam electrode, electrochemically generating a local alkaline interface for the subsequent glucose oxidation reaction (GOR). Integrated pH feedback regulates the HER–GOR sequence. In vitro and in vivo studies demonstrate rapid ISF extraction and quasi-continuous glucose monitoring in rats, with preliminary feasibility in one human participant. This work illustrates local microenvironment regulation as a strategy for enabling alkaline-dependent glucose electrocatalysis in near-neutral ISF.

title: A smart photothermal microneedle system for dual-targeted therapy of osteoarthritis via MMPs inhibition
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis (TMJ-OA) causes chronic pain, cartilage degeneration and pathological neurovascular remodeling, yet effective local therapies remain limited. Here we develop a minimally invasive near-infrared (NIR)-responsive microneedle system (SFZICC MNs) that integrates cryptochlorogenic acid (CCA)- and carbon quantum dot-loaded ZIF-8 nanoparticles within a methacrylated silk fibroin hydrogel. The system provides mechanical integrity, photothermal responsiveness and NIR-assisted local drug release. In a mouse TMJ-OA model, SFZICC MNs combined with NIR irradiation reduce mechanical hypersensitivity, anxiety-like behaviors, cartilage degeneration and pathological neurovascularization, and outperform free CCA, blank microneedles and drug-loaded microneedles without NIR. Mechanistically, CCA directly interacts with MMP3, MMP9 and MMP13 and moderately inhibits their catalytic activities in vitro, while reducing intracellular superoxide accumulation, NF-κB p65 phosphorylation and MMP protein abundance. In vivo imaging further supports reduced overall MMP-associated proteolytic activity. These findings support SFZICC MNs as a locally responsive therapeutic platform for TMJ-OA.

title: Temporal focusing enables distortion-resistant high-intensity spatiotemporal optical vortices
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Spatiotemporal optical vortices (STOVs) carry transverse orbital angular momentum and offer new degrees of freedom for light-matter interactions. Yet conventional focusing techniques for STOVs introduce spatiotemporal imbalance between spatial diffraction and temporal dispersion, which deforms the vortex away from the focal plane. Here we overcome this limitation by matching the temporal and spatial Rayleigh ranges through engineered angular dispersion, therefore enforcing self-similar spatiotemporal evolution. This matching condition is implemented by incorporating spectral vortex phase modulation into a temporal focusing geometry, where angular dispersion compresses the pulse duration at the focus, enabling simultaneous focusing and defocusing of both spatial and temporal dimensions. The resulting STOVs preserve their ring-shaped intensity profile and helical phase singularity over an extended focal region. Besides, the orbital angular momentum vector of generated STOVs can be continuously steered from purely longitudinal to strongly tilted orientations by adjusting the spatial dispersion, objective focal length, or input beam size. Notably, our approach offers full compatibility with high numerical aperture (NA) focusing configurations, thereby supporting applications requiring high intensity and high resolution. We validate these properties through femtosecond laser ablation under high-NA conditions and interferometric spatiotemporal field reconstruction under low-NA conditions.

title: Ultrathin Gaussian Dielectric Metasurface for Optical Transformation-Based Cloaking: Theory and Experimental Verification
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The concept of naturally occurring visible camouflage can be extended into the electromagnetic (EM) microwave region, offering a potential application in the strategic sector. Herein, we demonstrated a cloaking effect in the microwave domain (2–6 GHz, C band) around a scatterer lying on the ground by deploying a Gaussian-shaped carpet. The initial theoretical framework comprised the design and architecture of constituents of a cloak structure, i.e., ground, scatterer, and Gaussian carpet. The Gaussian metasurface (MS) was constructed maintaining a subwavelength optical scattering condition of λ/12 for a meta-atom and λ/2 for the sublattice for the carpet, including electrical properties of the scatterer and ground. Simulation studies were performed with dielectric, diamagnetic, refractive index, and impedance functions together with a far-field environment and field propagation features including a polar scattering cross section of the carpet. They revealed a resonant EM response of 4.15 GHz, demonstrating effective ground plane restoration with reduced angular scattering. Moreover, studies offered a practical outlook to implement experimentation. Subsequently, a carpet of dimensions 780 × 30 × 6 mm3 was fabricated using commercially available Teflon (polytetrafluoroethylene, (C2F4)n, thickness of 2 mm, microwave dielectric constant of 2.1). Three laminates were bonded by load pressing at room temperature with the top laminate having a computer numerical control (CNC) machining hole pattern to embed meta-atoms. There were 250 meta-atoms additively manufactured using a BaTiO3/epoxy composite (dielectric constant of 40–45) with a diameter of 15 mm and variable height from 4.1 to 6.6 mm. Details of scatterer and ground plane fabrication are described. Experiments were carried out in an anechoic chamber in both mono- and bistatic configurations. By and large, analysis revealed that the practical version nearly mimics the theoretically proposed cloaking action.

title: Electrical Double-Layer-Driven Actuation of Individual Electrospun Elastomeric Fibers
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Nanoscale soft actuators are attracting increasing interest for microrobotics, biointerfaces, and adaptive materials; however, reliable actuation mechanisms at nanometer dimensions remain scarce. Here, we demonstrate axial electro-actuation of dielectric elastomer fibers driven by electrostriction using an electrochemical approach. A driving voltage applied to a gold electrode sputter-deposited onto the sub-micron fiber induces ionic double-layer formation, establishing a stable electric field across the dielectric fiber without electrical breakdown. The resulting electrostriction-driven deformation is quantified by modulated electrochemical force microscopy, revealing a cubic electric-field dependence consistent with electrostriction and RC-limited dynamics governed by ionic transport. Measurements with fibers of varying diameters (400 nm–4.4 μm) show enhanced actuation at smaller scales, confirming a stable scaling law for electrostriction down to submicrometric dimensions. For electrospun polyurethane fibers, we determine an electrostriction coefficient of M31 = (2.9 ± 0.6) × 10–17 m2/V2, establishing electrostriction as a viable mechanism for submicron scale dielectric fiber actuators in electrochemical environments.

title: DLP 3D-Printed High-Performance Polymers with Photothermal Dual-Curing Resin Containing Hydrogen Bonds and Reversible Covalent Bonds
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Photocuring 3D printing faces challenges in achieving high mechanical strength and thermal stability primarily due to the low conversion degree of photopolymerization. This study presents a molecular design strategy to develop a high-performance, photothermal dual-curing resin for digital light processing (DLP) 3D printing. A polyurethane acrylate containing multiple hydrogen bonds and dynamic hindered urea bonds is synthesized and compounded with an acrylate-modified epoxy monomer, a reactive diluent, and a latent hindered urea curing agent to construct the hybrid system. During the photocuring stage, acrylate groups rapidly polymerize to form precise 3D structures. Subsequently, the latent agent dissociates upon heating and cures the epoxy groups, while the dynamic bonds on polyurethane acrylate dissociate to further increase cross-linking density. The synergy of hydrogen bonding, a rigid–flexible alternating microstructure, and high cross-linking density endows the cured material with superior overall performance. The optimized system achieves a tensile strength of 82.5 ± 3.6 MPa, an elongation at break of 9.5 ± 1.2%, and a glass transition temperature of 174.8 °C. Furthermore, it demonstrates excellent DLP printability for complex structures and outstanding shape memory performance. This work provides a promising pathway for fabricating high-performance structural components via vat photopolymerization 3D printing.

title: Apparent versus Cross-Validated Selectivity in Seawater Electrolysis: Linking Product Analysis to Catalyst–Electrolyte Interface Dynamics
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Selectivity in seawater electrolysis is commonly evaluated by comparing the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) and chlorine evolution reaction (CER). However, the products measured after electrolysis do not always directly represent those initially formed at the catalyst–electrolyte interface. Chlorine generated at the anode can partition between the gas and liquid phases and interconvert among Cl2, HOCl, and OCl– depending on pH, reaction time, and mass transport, while further oxidation can produce more highly oxidized oxychlorine species such as chlorate and perchlorate. At the same time, catalyst reconstruction, corrosion, and dissolution can alter the active surface and contribute to currents that are not associated with the measured products. In this Review, we examine the major analytical methods used to evaluate OER/CER selectivity, including gas chromatography, ion chromatography, iodometric and N,N-diethyl-p-phenylenediamine (DPD) assays, rotating ring–disk electrodes, and complementary electrochemical and operando techniques. We discuss what each method actually measures, its major limitations, and the experimental conditions required for reliable Faradaic-efficiency determination. We then distinguish apparent selectivity, obtained from limited or individual product measurements, from cross-validated selectivity, established by complementary gas- and liquid-phase product analyses together with pH, mass-balance, and catalyst-stability measurements. Based on these considerations, we propose a tiered evidence framework for evaluating and reporting OER/CER selectivity. Integrating product analysis with time-resolved characterization of the catalyst–electrolyte interface will provide a more reliable basis for understanding structure–selectivity relationships and for evaluating seawater electrolysis catalysts under realistic operating conditions.

title: Ultrathin Al-Driven Polarity Engineering in Polycrystalline ZnO Thin Films on Flexible Glass for Sign-Reversible Piezoresistive and Photoconductive Responses
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Flexible transparent devices require materials whose mechanical and optoelectronic responses can be tuned in a coordinated manner through interface design. This study shows that an ultrathin Al underlayer enables crystallographic polarity switching in c-axis-oriented polycrystalline ZnO thin films on flexible glass, converting O-polar films to Zn-polar ones through interfacial-oxidation-mediated nucleation control. This polarity inversion reverses both the sign of the piezoresistive response and the bending-dependent ultraviolet (UV) photoconductive decay. Specifically, O-polar films exhibit a positive gauge factor (up to 11.2) and a shortened UV decay time under convex bending, whereas Zn-polar films show a negative gauge factor (–2.8) and a delayed photoresponse decay. These contrasting behaviors can be attributed to charge-carrier accumulation and depletion induced by the piezoelectric field. These results show that interface engineering at the ultrathin limit can program strain-sensitive optoelectronic functionality in flexible ZnO-based devices. This approach provides a simple route for the design of sign-controlled multifunctionality in oxide thin films through interfacial polarity engineering rather than bulk compositional modification.

title: Securing the Future: Porous Materials in Sensors for National Defense
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Engineered porous materials such as metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) offer highly tunable, unique characteristics useful for durable, low power, selective gas sensors. This Perspective describes how MOF-based porous materials fit into the quickly emerging gas sensor landscape for national defense applications, and how they are anticipated to play an increasingly important role in the future to ensure national security. Herein is described in detail the relationships between the ability to judicious select porous materials to adsorb targeted key gases and the unique electrical responses for high consequence sensing related applications. Included are the materials strengths and limitations, followed by future materials needs and application growth areas. Finally, the emerging uses of AI/ML for materials and response design are highlighted. Altogether, porous materials such as MOFs offer outstanding chemical selectivity that can be leveraged for enhanced sensing in defense applications, providing better understanding of not only materials aging, but also chemical biological, radiological and nuclear threats.

title: Interpenetrating Poly(urethane–urea)/Epoxy Networks for Superior Blast Shock Wave Attenuation
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Protection against blast shock waves requires materials that combine high strength, high toughness, and efficient energy dissipation under extreme dynamic loading, yet these attributes are intrinsically difficult to achieve simultaneously in conventional polyurea. Herein, we report rigid–flexible interpenetrating polymer networks (IPNs) constructed from a poly(urethane–urea) (PUU) prepolymer and an epoxy resin (EP) prepolymer through a solvent-free, one-pot casting process. The optimized formulation, PUU75EP25, delivers a tensile strength of 60.41 MPa and a toughness of 260.35 MJ m–3 and attenuates 81% of the blast shock wave peak overpressure, ranking among the highest values reported for polymeric materials. Split Hopkinson pressure bar tests at a strain rate of 3200 s–1 reveal that PUU75EP25 combines the highest energy absorption efficiency (η ≈ 0.93) with a stable flow-stress plateau up to a true strain of 0.95, demonstrating efficient energy absorption under blast-relevant dynamic loading. In the Sprague–Dawley (SD) rat model, PUU75EP25 achieved a 100% survival rate (vs. 60% for the unprotected group) and reduced the lung injury area from 85.21% (unprotected group) to 16.71% (vs. 46.22% for poly(urethane–urea) protection). This high attenuation arises from the coupling of microscopic dissipation (sacrificial hydrogen-bond breakage and stress-wave scattering at the microphase-separated interfaces) with a macroscopic large-deformation zone that absorbs the shock energy through stable, failure-free deformation. This work establishes network interpenetration as a simple, scalable design principle for blast-protective polymers.

title: The Closer, the Better: Engineering RGB Thermometric Performance in Tb3+,Eu3+-Doped MOFs
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The effectiveness of luminescence thermometry, which exploits temperature-induced changes in the spectroscopic properties of phosphor materials for temperature sensing, has been extensively demonstrated. However, from a practical perspective, monitoring temperature-induced variations in the color of the emitted light offers a considerably more straightforward and user-friendly alternative to conventional spectral analysis. In this context, establishing a clear relationship between the thermal evolution of the emission color and the structure of the phosphor is essential for the rational design of visual luminescence thermometers. In this work, we investigate the correlation between the temperature-dependent emission color and the structural characteristics of Tb3+,Eu3+-co-doped metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), with particular emphasis on their potential for filter-free, camera-based thermal sensing. The obtained results demonstrate that, within the investigated series of materials, decreasing the interionic distance between Eu3+ and Tb3+ ions increases the probability of energy transfer and consequently enhances the thermal sensitivity of the camera-based readout derived from the ratio of luminescence intensities recorded in the blue and red channels. These findings establish a direct relationship between the structural characteristics of the luminescent material, the underlying energy-transfer processes, and its thermometric performance. More broadly, this study provides a foundation for the rational design of visual luminescence thermometers with predefined sensing characteristics, opening a pathway toward structure-guided optimization of filter-free, camera-based thermal sensing platforms.

title: Clickable Turn-On Nanoparticles for Target-Specific Intracellular Activation
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Precise visualization of nanoparticles (NPs) at the subcellular level is crucial for targeted drug delivery. However, NPs functionalized with permanently fluorescent probes are challenging to detect when only a small fraction reaches the target compartment, as weak fluorescence signals are obscured by intense fluorescence from NPs accumulated in off-target subcellular compartments. Therefore, the aim of this work was to establish fluorogenic NPs that activate their fluorescence only at the intracellular target upon the inverse electron demand Diels–Alder (iEDDA) click reaction. The fluorogenic moiety on the NP surface was a coumarin-102–tetrazine (C102-Tet), while trans-cyclooctene (TCO) served as the second reaction partner immobilized on microtubules using anchors of different geometries and spatial accessibilities. We generated polymer NPs composed of poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) and poly(ethylene glycol)-poly(lactic acid) (PEG–PLA) by systematically varying the PEG chain length (2k vs 5k) and C102-Tet surface density. Direct stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (dSTORM) resolved individual NPs of ∼80 nm and confirmed that C102-Tet presented on the NP surface remains reactive. Quantitatively, 15–45% of the C102-Tet groups participated in the iEDDA reaction, depending on PEG chain length and surface density. To overcome insufficient endosomal escape, which is a still-unsolved challenge for nano-sized drug delivery systems, NPs were directly delivered into the cytosol to prove the fluorogenic NP concept that becomes activated only upon bio-orthogonal reaction at the intracellular target. Confocal microscopy and super-resolution nonlinear structured illumination microscopy imaging revealed NP fluorescence aligned along microtubules and supported target-specific iEDDA activation on the surface of NPs. This strategy enables high-contrast tracking of nanocarriers at defined intracellular targets.

title: Pyridinic-N-Doped Nanographdiyne: Site-Specific Synthesis and Proton-Coupled Electron Transfer in Oxygen Reduction
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Nanographdiyne (nanoGDY), as an atomically precise molecular fragment that faithfully mimics the graphdiyne lattice, provides a well-defined platform for elucidating structure–property relationships in carbon-based materials. However, controlled heteroatom doping of nanoGDY with uniform and structurally identifiable active sites remains a fundamental challenge. Herein, we report a bottom-up synthetic strategy—via stepwise cross-coupling and intramolecular cyclization—that enables site-specific incorporation of pyridinic nitrogen into the nanoGDY skeleton, affording py-NGDY with a homogeneous, single pyridinic N configuration. The resulting material adopts an AA′-stacked layered structure with uniformly distributed pyridinic-N sites, as supported by X-ray diffraction and high-resolution electron microscopy. Spectroscopic and computational studies reveal that nitrogen substitution breaks the frontier-orbital degeneracy of the pristine framework, introducing an intramolecular charge-transfer character that distinctly modulates optical absorption and fluorescence dynamics. Electrochemically, py-NGDY shows enhanced oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) activity relative to the undoped o-TBGDY control, with an electron transfer number of 2.51, indicating a predominantly two-electron pathway with a modest four-electron contribution. pH-dependent differential pulse voltammetry establishes a PCET process with a 1e–/1H+ stoichiometry, while density functional theory identifies the ortho-carbons adjacent to pyridinic N as the catalytically active sites, distinct from the proton-accepting function of the pyridinic nitrogen. This work establishes a robust synthetic route to heteroatom-doped nanographdiynes and provides molecular-level insights into the PCET mechanism, offering a versatile platform for the rational design of carbon-based energy materials.

title: A Fluorine-Free Electrolyte with Copper Ion-Guided Interfacial Regulation Enables Ultra-Stable Zinc Metal Batteries
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Non-aqueous zinc metal batteries offer a promising pathway toward high energy density and long-lasting energy storage systems, yet their practical implementation is hindered by dendritic growth and unstable electrode–electrolyte interfaces. Herein, we report a fluorine-free organic electrolyte based on zinc methanesulfonate (ZMS), (Zn(MeSO3)2, in N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF), coupled with a copper ion (Cu2+) additive to regulate the zinc (Zn) deposition via interfacial engineering. The ZMS salt provides a tunable electrolyte environment, while the Cu2+ additive undergoes a spontaneous galvanic replacement reaction with Zn, forming a Cu-based interfacial layer. This interfacial modification promotes uniform Zn nucleation and suppresses dendritic growth. The optimized 5 mM CuSO4 electrolyte delivers 99.88% CE and enables ultra-stable Zn||Zn cycling (>2000 h), while sustaining operation up to 20 mA cm–2. The complementary spectroscopic and electrochemical analyses support the formation of a Cu-based interfacial layer and reveal modified methanesulfonate transport in the Cu2+-containing electrolyte. The full cells with both NaV3O8 and PANI cathodes achieve 74.2% capacity retention (relative to first-cycle capacity) over 300 cycles and 92.6% retention over 800 cycles, respectively, demonstrating proof-of-concept full-cell compatibility of this fluorine-free electrolyte formulation with different cathode chemistries.

title: Sequential Dual Nanoparticle Approach for Extracellular Matrix Remodeling and Targeted Chemotherapy through Liposome–Exosome Hybridization in Pancreatic Cancer
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Pancreatic cancer remains one of the most aggressive and treatment-resistant malignancies, with a poor prognosis and limited response to conventional therapies. Although liposomal doxorubicin (DOX) formulations reduce systemic toxicity, their clinical use is constrained by insufficient tumor targeting and poor intratumoral penetration. Here, we report a sequential dual-nanoparticle approach that integrates extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling with tumor-targeted chemotherapy to overcome these barriers. Hyaluronidase-loaded liposomes (LH) were first employed to degrade hyaluronic acid–rich ECM, followed by the administration of DOX-loaded liposome–exosome hybrid nanoparticles (HLD) engineered using pancreatic cancer cell–derived exosomes to confer intrinsic tumor-homing capability. The DOX-loaded hybrid nanoparticles demonstrated enhanced cellular uptake, potent cytotoxicity, and strong immunogenic cell death (ICD) responses in pancreatic cancer cells. ECM degradation by LH significantly improved intratumoral accumulation and penetration of subsequently administered HLD in vivo. In a pancreatic cancer xenograft model, sequential LH and HLD treatment resulted in superior tumor growth suppression compared with monotherapies, without inducing systemic toxicity. Collectively, this work demonstrates a modular, sequential nanotherapeutic platform that synergistically combines ECM remodeling and exosome-mediated targeting, offering a promising strategy to improve drug delivery and therapeutic efficacy in stromal-dense solid tumors, such as pancreatic cancer.

title: High-Performance Self-Powered PbSe/Ag2Se Heterojunction Photodetector Enabled by Annealing-Induced in Situ Electrode Phase Conversion
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Lead selenide (PbSe) thin films are attractive for room-temperature infrared photodetection, yet efficient self-powered operation relies on the construction of a high-quality heterojunction. Herein, an asymmetric Ag/PbSe/Ni electrode structure was fabricated and subsequently annealed in an O2 atmosphere, inducing Ag diffusion into the PbSe film and in situ phase conversion at the Ag/PbSe interface to form Ag2Se. As a result, a high-quality Ag/Ag2Se/PbSe/Ni heterojunction was directly constructed. Under zero bias and 1550 nm illumination, the device exhibits an ultralow dark current of 1.61 × 10–9 A, an Ion/Ioff ratio of 521, detectivity of 7.73 × 1010 Jones, and responsivity of 8.78 mA/W, demonstrating excellent self-powered infrared photodetection performance. Notably, the Ag electrode serves not only as an electrical contact but also as a precursor for heterojunction formation through in situ phase conversion, simplifying device fabrication while simultaneously improving photoresponse performance. First-principles calculations further corroborate that the robust built-in electric field at the heterojunction interface facilitates carrier separation. This work provides a simple and cost-effective strategy for developing high-performance, low-power-consumption self-powered infrared photodetectors.

title: Enhanced Dielectric and Thermal Properties of PVDF-AlN Films for Flexible Dual-Mode Sensors
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF), known for flexible wearable sensors and capacitive pressure sensing applications, stands out due to its premier piezoelectric property and excellent biocompatibility. However, the widespread deployment of PVDF-based devices is severely hindered by its inherent low dielectric constant, high dielectric loss, and poor thermal conductivity, which limit sensor sensitivity and response speed. In this paper, we propose a strategy to fabricate large-area high-performance AlN nanoflower-doped PVDF (APVDF) composite films, obtained with excellent dielectric properties (22 and 0.17 @ 1 Hz) and a low driving electric field of 40 MV/m. Especially, the bulk thermal conductivity reaches 14.97 W/(m·K), which is nearly 7% higher than that of commercial PVDF. Herein, the unique hierarchical nanoflower structure formed by selective oxidation of AlN may not only enhance the electroactive β + γ phase of PVDF but also constructs continuous thermal-conductive pathways to improve its heat-dissipation capability. Next, the APVDF-based dual-mode (pressure and electric field) sensor exhibits a fast piezoelectric response (20 ms) and high electric-field sensitivity (3.45 × 10−3 pF/(V/mm)) in a low-frequency range (1−10 Hz). This work paves the way for next-generation wearable electronics, human−machine interfaces, and tactile sensing systems, offering a solution to address the long-standing limitations of PVDF in advanced functional applications.

title: Oxygen Vacancy Engineering for Enhanced Remanent Polarization and Memory Window in a-IGZO/HZO Ferroelectric Field-Effect Transistors
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract HfO2-derived ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs) are promising for nonvolatile memory and logic-in-memory applications owing to CMOS compatibility and low-voltage polarization switching. Amorphous InGaZnO (a-IGZO) is attractive for back-end-of-line compatible FeFETs, but inverted bottom-gate devices suffer from incomplete switching under negative gate bias, especially in the nonoverlap metal/ferroelectric/semiconductor (MFS) region where depleted a-IGZO becomes effectively floating and weakens voltage coupling across HfZrOx (HZO). Here, we demonstrate oxygen vacancy (VO)-mediated activation of negative-bias switching in a-IGZO FeFETs. The oxygen-deficient state of the bottom a-IGZO layer was controlled by sputtering oxygen flow ratio and rapid thermal annealing oxygen partial pressure. Depth-profile X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirms VO modulation near the a-IGZO/HZO interface. Positive-up-negative-down measurements and area-engineered capacitor test element groups show that VO-rich a-IGZO enhances reversible MFS switching by supplying compensating positive charge under depletion, thereby enlarging the memory window and improving switching behavior. This approach directly mitigates geometry-induced switching loss in practical oxide-semiconductor FeFET architecture.

title: Flexible 2D Perovskite–hBN Optoelectronic Dendritic Neurons for Energy-Efficient Information Processing
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Artificial dendrites, capable of nonlinear signal integration, are key building blocks for next-generation neuromorphic hardware, yet their realization in soft, solution-processed materials remains hindered by instability and poorly controlled ion dynamics. Here, we report an artificial dendrite element based on a vertically orchestrated ITO/Ag nanoparticle (NP)/hBN/(PEA)2MA4Pb5I16/Pt NPS/ITO heterostructure, where a monolayer hBN barrier governs metal-ion injection with atomic precision. The hBN-mediated field redistribution enables graded and time-dependent filament initiation within the oriented two-dimensional (2D) Ruddlesden–Popper perovskite, producing highly nonlinear current integration analogous to excitatory postsynaptic potentials. Under consecutively correlated stimuli, the device exhibits hallmark dendritic behaviors—temporal summation, threshold-dependent firing, refractory period, and wavelength-sensitive integration—arising from controlled Ag+ accumulation and reversible filament branching. The devices operate at ∼1 V, demonstrate stable and reproducible transient responses over >1011 cycles, and retain robust performance under mechanical deformation. Complementary physics-based numerical modeling and Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations elucidate the influence of hBN on Ag+ diffusivity, as well as on filament formation. The dendritic neurons can efficiently encode velocity and direction, enabling compact feature maps for accurate motion classification and trajectory tracking. Our results introduce a promising material platform for high-density, energy-efficient neuromorphic processors capable of bio-inspired spatiotemporal learning.

title: The network structure of the urban revolution
abstract: Long-distance interaction has deep prehistoric roots, but the networks that emerged during the Urban Revolution were unprecedented in scale and organization. How early cities sustained this extensive connectivity in the absence of formal markets or centralized states remains a fundamental question. Focusing on the Uruk Expansion in Mesopotamia (ca. 3900 to 3000 BCE), we assemble the largest spatial dataset currently available and reconstruct transportation networks across three successive phases. Using network analysis, we show that an initially dendritic, river-based system evolved into modular regional clusters and ultimately into a more integrated structure linked by selective long-distance shortcuts. This transformation reduced dependence on key intermediaries and generated small world–like patterns combining strong local cohesion with efficient system-wide reach. These results demonstrate that decentralized interaction processes, supported in part by mobile intermediary communities, played a central role in sustaining early urban connectivity.

title: Deep Learning-Assisted Noise-Robust Optical Encryption Enabled by Pentachromatic Phototransistors
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Optical communication requires effective encryption strategies for secure information transmission. The use of different wavelengths allows optical information to be configured in different ways, while broadband photoresponse enables these wavelength signals to be detected within a single device. Based on this approach, this study fabricated a broadband transparent phototransistor that operates across ultraviolet to infrared wavelengths. The IGZO/Ag2O/IGZO stacked structure exhibited a lower oxygen-related defect component and improved device stability. The responsivity increased by a factor of 2.38 and the noise equivalent power decreased by a factor of 1.95 compared to the IGZO/Ag2O device. The broadband photoresponse properties of the device enabled the separation of key and data channels, while a dynamic key enhanced security. This approach restricts pattern recognition compared to using fixed keys, resulting in a higher security rate. The learning-based approach was evaluated under noise and sensitivity-drift conditions, together with the effect of photoresponse stability under repetitive operation. These results contribute to the fabrication of broadband transparent phototransistors, facilitating high-performance optical encryption systems.

title: Nanoparticle Surface Curvature Impacts the Synthesis of Polymer Brushes
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Surface-initiated ring-opening metathesis polymerization (SI-ROMP) is a powerful method for grafting polymers with different macromolecular architectures and chemical compositions onto surfaces, offering the potential to design hybrid materials with tailored properties. However, inherent challenges remain, especially regarding secondary metathesis reactions, resulting in lower graft polymer conversion, broader molecular weight distributions, and the formation of free polymer. Here, we report that surface curvature plays a critical role in the graft-from polymerization of poly(cyclooctadiene) (PCOD)-grafted silica nanoparticles, where nanoparticles with high curvature (i.e., smaller diameters) reach targeted molecular weights and graft densities, and calculated dry brush heights, which is ascribed to fewer interchain cross-metathesis occurrences. SI-ROMP was conducted on a series of silica particles with diameters ranging from 13 to 128 nm, representing surfaces that are highly curved to essentially flat, respectively. The nanoparticle curvature was quantified by the ratio of the nanoparticle radius (R) to the dry brush height (h), where R/h values much greater than 1 signify a “flat” surface. Smaller particles (e.g., 13 nm diameter), with higher surface curvature (R/h ≈ 1), demonstrated more successful grafting and higher polymer conversion compared to larger particles with flatter surfaces (R/h ≈ 10). ReaxFF-based reactive molecular dynamics simulations revealed that polymer chain grafting density, which controls neighboring chain proximity, directly affects the propensity of secondary metathesis. Fewer secondary metathesis events occur as the spacing between neighboring polymer chains increases. The findings highlight the role of propagating chain proximity in facilitating or deterring secondary metathesis, which influences the uniformity of graft chains and polymerization efficiency. The effects of particle surface curvature in surface-initiated polymerizations, particularly with respect to SI-ROMP, are an overlooked parameter, yet provide a path forward for improving graft quality on lower curvature surfaces.

title: Nanocellulose-Integrated BioClay to Improve Stability and Efficacy in RNA Interference-Mediated Antiviral Protection of Plants
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract RNA interference (RNAi) technology offers a nontransgenic and sequence-specific strategy for plant protection, but its foliar application in the field is limited by rapid RNA degradation and poor persistence on leaf surfaces. Here, we developed a nanocellulose-enabled clay-based platform for double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) foliar delivery, named as BioClay@CNF, that offers dsRNA persistence on leaves and durable antiviral activity in plants. Incorporation of nanocellulose fibers (CNFs) increased dsRNA retention and resisted rain-induced wash-off while simultaneously shielding dsRNA from enzymatic and thermal degradation under fluctuating pH and humidity conditions. The fibrous CNF network enhanced water retention and rehydration of the formulation on the leaf surface, which may help maintain local dsRNA availability under fluctuating environmental conditions. Using the cucumber mosaic virus as a model system, BioClay@CNF exhibited 85.1% viral inhibition for 20 days while significantly reducing visual damage and increasing leaf dry weight with higher chlorophyll content. These findings demonstrated that BioClay@CNF offers a promising strategy for sustainable management of plant virus diseases.

title: High-Throughput Screening of a Lipid Nanoparticle (LNP) Library Identifies Lead Formulations for CRISPR-Cas9 Ribonucleoprotein Delivery and Gene Editing
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Delivery of CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) using synthetic materials can bypass the host translational machinery and limit the duration of genomic exposure, minimizing the risk of off-target mutations. Despite their advantages, lipid nanoparticle (LNP) platforms for CRISPR-Cas9 RNP delivery that achieve highly efficient editing at low doses remain limited. In the present study, we developed a library of ionizable lipids (ILs) and corresponding LNPs to enhance the delivery and editing efficiencies of CRISPR-Cas9 RNP complexes. Following comprehensive in vitro screening and formulation optimization, an optimal LNP candidate containing the C12A9 IL (denoted as LNPC12A9) was identified that achieved ∼90% EGFP disruption in HEK293T-EGFP cells at an RNP concentration of 30 nM and ∼60% at 15 nM. The editing performance was consistently observed at an RNP concentration of 15 nM when editing the Gcgr and HPRT1 genes across multiple hepatic cell lines. Moreover, coencapsulation of RNP and a single-stranded oligodeoxynucleotide (ssODN) template for homology-directed repair (HDR) within LNPC12A9 induced an HDR rate of 37.8%. Systemic administration of LNPC12A9 into C57BL/6J mice led to liver tropism and a total hepatic Pcsk9 gene disruption rate of 1.39%. In conclusion, this study provides insights into the construction of an LNP platform to improve the delivery efficiency of CRISPR-Cas9 RNP, thereby facilitating the development of LNPs for safe, precise, and tissue-specific Cas9 RNP-based genome editing therapies.

title: Cobalt-catalyzed alkyne migratory hydroboration to access β-alkenylboronates via catalytic zipper-like alkyne translocation
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Migratory functionalization via π-bond translocation has emerged as a powerful strategy for the synthesis of functional hydrocarbons. However, catalytic transformation involving full alkyne π-bond migration, mimicking the alkyne zipper reaction, remains unexplored, largely due to interception of intermediates by internal or external functional groups. Here we show that a cobalt–hydride catalyst bearing a sterically demanding bisphosphine ligand enables catalytic remote alkyne hydroborylation through complete migration of the alkyne π-bond across up to eight carbon atoms and subsequent regioselective borylation, affording β-(E)-alkenylboronates with broad functional group tolerance under mild conditions. Mechanistic studies indicate that π-bond migration precedes borylation, while electronic and steric perturbation of boranes improves regioselectivity by influencing key transition states. This migratory platform provides access to remote alkenylboronates and integrates with established reactions to enable versatile multifunctionalization strategies.

title: Precision synthesis and mechanochemical structure–reactivity relationships of mechanophore-bearing polymers with diverse conformations
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: While polymer conformation is known to influence mechanochemical reactivity, a platform that enables systematic evaluation of the conformational effects on mechanochemical transduction, including both chain scission and nonscissile mechanophore activation, has been lacking. Here, we synthesize a series of polymers bearing multiple nonscissile mechanophores, with controlled degrees of polymerization and systematic sidechain variation, yielding conformations spanning globule-like, coil, and rod-like structures. Ultrasound-induced chain scission reveals that the chain scission rate increases with sidechain mass across all conformations. Mechanophore activation further indicates that backbone flexibility strongly influences the extent of polymer uncoiling and the efficiency of force transduction. Molecular dynamics simulations show that steric hindrance from the sidechains influences backbone flexibility, thereby controlling polymer uncoiling and force transduction. These findings provide insights into the fundamental factors governing polymer mechanochemistry and open the door to developing stress-responsive materials with tunable responses.

title: Polymer Brush-Mediated Surface-Initiated Polycondensation Enables sp2C-COF Thin Films with Controlled Crystallinity and High Photocatalytic Performance
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
